title: Three intoxications
hookLine: the pride of youth, of health, of life (AN 3.38)

lines: THREE LOTUS PONDS, BLUE, RED, WHITE.
A WHITE SUNSHADE, DAY AND NIGHT.
cards: We've heard the palace story told about him: the sheltered prince, the four sights. In this short discourse from the Book of Threes, the Buddha tells it himself, in startling detail.
I was delicate, monks, he says, most delicate. At my father's home, lotus ponds were made just for me, one of blue lotuses, one of red, one of white. I wore only fine cloth from Kasi.
A white sunshade was held over me day and night, so cold and heat, dust and dew wouldn't touch me.

teach.h: THREE PALACES, ONE FOR EACH SEASON
teach.b: He had three palaces, one for winter, one for summer, one for the rains. In the rainy months he stayed in the rains palace, entertained by musicians, and didn't come down at all.
In other homes, he says, servants were fed broken rice with sour gruel; in his father's house, even the servants ate fine rice and meat. Even with all that, a thought came to me.

teach.h: DISGUST AT THE OLD, FORGETTING ONESELF
teach.b: An untaught person, himself subject to aging, sees someone old and feels disgust and shame, forgetting that he will age too. That isn't fitting for me. As he reflected, the intoxication of youth left him.
The same with illness: the untaught are repelled by the sick, though they'll fall ill too, and the intoxication of health left him. The same with death, and the intoxication of life left him.
The Pali word is mada, used for drunkenness and for the madness of pride. Youth, health, being alive: none of them are bad.
The intoxication is the feeling that they're mine to keep, and that the old, the sick and the dying are some other kind of person.

teach.h: MADA: DRUNK ON YOUTH, HEALTH, LIFE
teach.b: In the very next discourse he names what these three do: a person drunk on youth, health or life acts badly in body, speech and mind.

teach.h: THE SUNSHADE CAN'T KEEP IT OFF
teach.b: It's easy to see how; the intoxication whispers that there's plenty of time.
Not a lecture on aging, then: a man remembering the white sunshade, and the moment he saw it couldn't keep anything off him forever.

how: Buddhist teachers draw on this discourse when speaking about aging, illness and death, and some meditators reflect on all three as a way to loosen the pride of youth, health and life.

o: three vices of a careless king's court
three drinks the precepts warn against
the pride of youth, health and being alive

s: in AN 3.38 the Buddha tells of his sheltered youth himself
he describes the lotus ponds, the Kasi cloth, the white sunshade and the three palaces.
the discourse says youth, health and life are bad
the intoxication is the problem: the pride that forgets one will age, sicken and die.
the untaught feel disgust at the old, forgetting they will age too
seeing that, the Buddha says, the intoxication of youth left him.

games.q: you're a young prince with three palaces and a white sunshade held over you. you see someone old and feel a flash of disgust. what does AN 3.38 say comes next?
o: see that you're subject to aging too, and let the pride of youth go.
order the old person out of sight.
games.why: the Buddha says he reflected that disgust wasn't fitting for one who will age, and the intoxication of youth left him.

practice: Feel the body as it is today, the age it is, the health it has, the life that's in it, and let a little gratitude in for each.
Then notice, gently, whether one of the three has a grip of pride: I'm too young for that, I never get sick, there's always tomorrow.
Soften it with a plain thought, this too will change, held not with fear but with clearer, kinder eyes toward anyone older or sicker than you.

wordCard.voice: Three intoxications. In AN 3.38, the Buddha, remembering his sheltered youth, names the pride of youth, of health, and of life, and tells how each one left him. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali mada: intoxication, pride; yobbana-mada, arogya-mada, jivita-mada: of youth, health and life.

carryVoice: Your line: the three intoxications. Aging, sickness and death are my road too. That's day six hundred sixty-one.
